title: From downloads to discussions: leveraging Yet Another Positioning Solver (YAPS) and modern movement analyses to transform raw telemetry data into interpretable results
text:
Jonathan Rodemann (National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis, USA)
Sophia Costa (Florida International University, USA)
Jennifer Rehage (Florida International University, USA)



Welcome to our Acoustic Telemetry Pipeline workshop! The goal of this workshop is to familiarize participants with the concept of Yet Another Positioning Solver (YAPS), Hidden Markov Models (HMMs), and Integrated Step Selection Functions (iSSFs) while providing a workflow that participants can use to turn raw telemetry data into preliminary results. We will start the workshop by providing background, theory, and case studies on YAPS, HMMs, and iSSFs. We will then walkthrough the pipeline from raw data to results using R code. R scripts and data are provided to encourage participants to follow along and use this pipeline on their own acoustic data.

This workshop provides an example of a workflow for positional acoustic telemetry data. These data are collected in a receiver array that is set up so that pings from tags can be heard by more than one receiver. While manufacturers provide their own algorithms to solve for these positions, they are either solved by proprietary software or paid services that lack transparency. The YAPS algorithm was created to provide a transparent algorithm to solve for acoustic telemetry positions. Using a correlated random walk model trained with signal time of arrival, this algorithm has been shown to be highly accurate and suitable across multiple acoustic telemetry platforms and in many different aquatic environments. 
The analyses we are employing in this workshop are Hidden Markov Models and Integrated Step Selection Functions. HMMs are in a class of models that focus on the decomposition of movement into distinct underlying states. The time series that is input into the HMM consists of regular time interval coordinates of an animal’s location, which is broken down into step lengths (the Euclidean distance between the locations) and turn angle (the change of direction between the directions of travel). The model then uses these values to assign x number of states using maximum likelihood estimation. The model output includes the average and standard deviation of step length and turn angle for each state found, which can be used on the original data to assign states. 
iSSFs are a type of resource selection function, defined as a function that produces values that are proportional to the probability of use by an animal. These types of models are a popular method to determine and predict relative habitat selection by animals that evaluate the relationships between resource use (i.e., the units of area selected by an animal) and the environmental characteristics associated with each unit of area. iSSFs go one step further by utilizing the movement data to appropriately define resource availability by matching each “used step” with a set of “available steps” randomly sampled from a distribution of characteristics derived from observed steps. The main benefit of using iSSFs over another RSF framework (such as calculating habitat use from known observation points and a background of pseudo-absence points) is that they allow the distinguishing of effects of environmental variables not just on the selection, but the movement process as well.

R and RStudio
R and RStudio are separate downloads and installations. R is the underlying statistical computing environment, but using R alone is no fun. RStudio is a graphical integrated development environment (IDE) that makes using R much easier and more interactive. You need to install R before you install RStudio. In the sections below are the instructions for installing R and R Studio on your operating system.

Windows

If you already have R and RStudio installed

Open RStudio, and click on “Help” > “Check for updates”. If a new version is available, quit RStudio, and download the latest version for RStudio.
To check which version of R you are using, start RStudio and the first thing that appears in the console indicates the version of R you are running. Alternatively, you can type sessionInfo(), which will also display which version of R you are running. Go on the CRAN website and check whether a more recent version is available. If so, please download and install it. You can check here for more information on how to remove old versions from your system if you wish to do so.



If you don’t have R and RStudio installed

Download R from the CRAN website.
Run the .exe file that was just downloaded
Go to the RStudio download page
Under Installers select RStudio x.yy.zzz - Windows 10/11 (where x, y, and z represent version numbers)
Double click the file to install it
Once it’s installed, open RStudio to make sure it works and you don’t get any error messages.




macOS

If you already have R and RStudio installed

Open RStudio, and click on “Help” > “Check for updates”. If a new version is available, quit RStudio, and download the latest version for RStudio.
To check the version of R you are using, start RStudio and the first thing that appears on the terminal indicates the version of R you are running. Alternatively, you can type sessionInfo(), which will also display which version of R you are running. Go on the CRAN website and check whether a more recent version is available. If so, please download and install it.



If you don’t have R and RStudio installed

Download R from the CRAN website.
Select the .pkg file for the latest R version
Double click on the downloaded file to install R
It is also a good idea to install XQuartz (needed by some packages)
Go to the RStudio download page
Under Installers select RStudio x.yy.zzz - Mac OS X 10.15+ (64-bit) (where x, y, and z represent version numbers)
Double click the file to install RStudio
Once it’s installed, open RStudio to make sure it works and you don’t get any error messages.




Linux

Follow the instructions for your distribution from CRAN, they provide information to get the most recent version of R for common distributions. For most distributions, you could use your package manager (e.g., for Debian/Ubuntu run sudo apt-get install r-base, and for Fedora sudo yum install R), but we don’t recommend this approach as the versions provided by this are usually out of date. In any case, make sure you have at least R 3.3.1.
Go to the RStudio download page
Under Installers select the version that matches your distribution, and install it with your preferred method (e.g., with Debian/Ubuntu sudo dpkg -i   rstudio-x.yy.zzz-amd64.deb at the terminal).
Once it’s installed, open RStudio to make sure it works and you don’t get any error messages.

title: YAPS and Data filtering
text:
Calculating tracks
The most important part to set up for the HMMs is differentiating the tracks. This is where the second big decision comes in. How long do you wait between position before it is a new track? Depends on your array design, tag specifications, and the biology of your organism. We are using a cut-off of 5 minutes because our tags have an average burst interval of 20-40 seconds, meaning the fish would have to miss 10 detections (and therefore left the array).

#So now we know where we are in space. Let's now set up the tracks for the HMM analysis
#We are going to filter it even more so that each position we keep is calculated by detections heard by 2 or more receivers
dat20 <- data %>% dplyr::filter(nobs >= 2)

#Now we are going to create a column that allows us to identify the start of a new track
#for this exercise, we decided that if the fish was not detected for 5 minutes, a new track would be created
dat20t <- dat20 %>% group_by(tag) %>% mutate(trackstart = ifelse(as.numeric(unclass(ts)-unclass(lag(ts))) > 300, 'Y', 'N')) %>% ungroup()
dat20t[is.na(dat20t)] <- 'Y'

str(dat20t)

#create a function that numbers the tracks and inputs what track each row is in
tracknum1 <- function(x){

    if (x$trackstart[i] == 'Y'){

    } else {
      x$track[i] <- x$track[i-1]

title: YAPS and Data filtering
text:
YAPS position calculations
This is the general workflow for syncing receivers and running tracks in YAPS. We won’t be running this code in this workshop and in fact, this code does not work because the syncing fails. In reality, you need to play around with your sync data (including splitting up the time periods if there are “blackouts”, possibly removing receivers, and other adjustments) for the sync model to be successful. We will pick up the workshop with the positions that were calculated by the developer of YAPS (WOW!), Henrik Baktoft.

#load libraries
#Install and load required libraries
install.packages(c(‘tidyverse’, ‘devtools’, ‘TMB’))
library(devtools)
library(tidyverse)
library(TMB)
devtools::install_github(“baktoft/yaps”)
library(yaps)
options(digits.secs = 3)
#test to make sure YAPS will work
testYaps()
#load data
vue <- data.table::fread(‘data/detections.csv’, fill=TRUE)
hydros <- data.table::fread(‘data/hydros.csv’, fill=TRUE)
detections <- prepDetections(raw_dat = vue, type=‘vemco_vue’)
detections <- detections %>% dplyr::filter(!is.na(frac))
#now we have our 2 datasets needed!
#sync hydrophones/ #set parameters
max_epo_diff <- 140 #Should be a little less than half of your shortest sync tag delay (ours are 6 - 10 minute)
min_hydros <- 4 #minimum amount of hydrophones needed for each sync tag ping to be heard on. Start high, then go low
time_keeper_idx <- 13 #Receiver with the “best clock”
fixed_hydros_idx <- c(3, 7:8, 11, 13:17, 20:21) #Receivers that have the best known positions. The more, the better
n_offset_day <- 2 #1 or 2
n_ss_day <- 2 #number of times you want the model to calculate speed of sound a day. 2 is good, best to use water temp if you have it
keep_rate <- 75 #number of sync tag detections for each hydro X offset_idx combinations to keep. Keeps the model doable
#compile list of dataframes
RYAPS <- list(hydros, detections)
names(RYAPS) <- c(‘hydros’, ‘detections’)
RYAPS$hydros$sync_tag <- as.double(RYAPS$hydros$sync_tag)
RYAPS$detections$tag <- as.integer(RYAPS$detections$tag)
RYAPS$detections$epo <- as.integer(RYAPS$detections$epo)
RYAPS$detections$serial <- as.integer(RYAPS$detections$serial)

#compile data for syncing
inp_sync <- getInpSync(sync_dat = RYAPS, max_epo_diff, min_hydros, time_keeper_idx, fixed_hydros_idx, n_offset_day, n_ss_day, keep_rate)
#check if it is good
getSyncCoverage(inp_sync, plot=T)
#we are good. Let’s try syncing
sync_model <- getSyncModel(inp_sync, silent=TRUE)
#check quality of synchronization
plotSyncModelResids(sync_model, by=‘overall’)
plotSyncModelResids(sync_model, by=‘sync_tag’)
plotSyncModelResids(sync_model, by=‘hydro’)
plotSyncModelCheck(sync_model, by=“sync_bin_sync”)
plotSyncModelCheck(sync_model, by=“sync_bin_hydro”)
plotSyncModelCheck(sync_model, by=“sync_tag”)
plotSyncModelCheck(sync_model, by=“hydro”)
#success! there is only a problem of 6 using SHYAPS1. I think it is fine. save it
save(sync_model, file = ‘sync_model_4’)
#apply sync model to detection data
detections_synced <- applySync(toa=RYAPS$detections, hydros=RYAPS$hydros, sync_model)
#Now that you have the sync model, run the tracks
#use the estimated positions of hydros
hydros_yaps <- data.table::data.table(sync_model$pl$TRUE_H)
colnames(hydros_yaps) <- c(‘hx’,‘hy’,‘hz’)
#specify focal tag
focal_tag <- 34507
rbi_min <- 20
rbi_max <- 40
#extract relevant tag data from detections
synced_dat_34507 <- detections_synced[tag == focal_tag]
#compile TOA matrix
toa_YAPS_34507 <- getToaYaps(synced_dat_34507, hydros_yaps, rbi_min, rbi_max, pingType=‘rbi’)
#compile all input data needed
inp_YAPS <- getInp(hydros_yaps, toa_YAPS_34507, E_dist=“Mixture”, n_ss=3, pingType=“rbi”, sdInits=1, rbi_min=rbi_min, rbi_max=rbi_max, ss_data_what=“est”, ss_data=0)
inp_YAPS$datTmb$rbi_min
inp_YAPS$params$top
min(diff(inp_YAPS$params$top))
checkInp(inp_YAPS)
#run YAPS!
yaps_out_34507 <- runYaps(inp_SAPS, silent=F)
plotYaps(yaps_out_34507)

section: Interpolation of tracks to a regular time interval
text:
Interpolation of tracks to a regular time interval
Hidden Markov Models require the data to have a regular time step. Because these positions are calculated from random burst tags, we need to interpolate the tracks to a regular interval. This is the third big decision - how do you parse out the time interval to interpolate the tracks? Our suggestion is to start at twice the average burst interval of the tag to account for possible missed detections.

#store the columns needed for this step
ts_col <- "ts"
id_col <- "tag"
track_col <- "track"
x_col <- "x"
y_col <- "y"

#Create a function that interpolates the tracks from the positions. For this function to work, you need to group the data before running it into unique ID X track combinations

interpolate_track <- function(df_group, dt_seconds = 180) { #The default time of the interpolated tracks is 3 minutes, but you can change that
  # df must contain columns: ts, x, y, plus id/track identifiers
  if (nrow(df_group) < 2) return(NULL)  # can't interpolate single-point tracks
  
  tmin <- min(df_group$ts, na.rm = TRUE)
  tmax <- max(df_group$ts, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  new_times <- seq(from = tmin, to = tmax, by = dt_seconds) #sequence the track out to regular intervals based on your start and end times and the interval you identify in the function
  if (length(new_times) < 2) return(NULL)
  
  # numeric times for approx - makes math easier
  orig_t_num <- as.numeric(df_group$ts)
  new_t_num <- as.numeric(new_times)
  
  # ensure sorted by time - earliest to latest
  ord <- order(orig_t_num)
  orig_t_num <- orig_t_num[ord]
  x_orig <- df_group[[x_col]][ord]
  y_orig <- df_group[[y_col]][ord]
  
  # linear interpolation (NA handling: approx requires finite values) - takes actual points and times, then interpolates the point between the actual points based on actual times
  ok_x <- is.finite(x_orig) & is.finite(orig_t_num)
  ok_y <- is.finite(y_orig) & is.finite(orig_t_num)
  if (!any(ok_x) || !any(ok_y)) return(NULL)
  
  x_interp <- approx(x = orig_t_num[ok_x], y = x_orig[ok_x], xout = new_t_num, rule = 2)$y #The y extracts only the interpolated points
  y_interp <- approx(x = orig_t_num[ok_y], y = y_orig[ok_y], xout = new_t_num, rule = 2)$y

  tibble(
    ts = new_times, #interpolated times
    !!id_col := df_group[[id_col]][1],
    !!track_col := df_group[[track_col]][1],
    x = x_interp,
    y = y_interp
  )
}

#Now let's run it on our data!

interp_df <- bind_rows(interp_list) #make dataframe
interp_df <- interp_df %>% mutate(ID = paste(tag, track, sep = "_")) #make ID column

section: Determining the initial step lengths and turn angles for the model
text:
Determining the initial step lengths and turn angles for the model
We have prepped our data. However, it is still not just plug and play. We need to investigate our data to fit general curves to our data to inform the model. We don’t need to do this, but it creates a more informed model based on the original data. We are trying to fit these data into two behavioral states, so we will want to inform the model with 2 curves.

curve(dgamma(x, shape = 1.5, rate=0.9), n=200, add=TRUE, col="royalblue", lwd=4) #shape is how right-skewed the gamma curve is
curve(dgamma(x, shape = 1.9, rate=0.7), n=200, add=TRUE, col="cadetblue", lwd=4) #rate is how tall the curve apex is
curve(dgamma(x, shape = 2.2, rate=0.4), n=200, add=TRUE, col="navyblue", lwd=4)

The second curve does not really add any more information either than including the step lengths that are longer.     step = pmin(step, quantile(step, 0.99, na.rm = TRUE))
  )

title: HMMs
section: Determining the initial step lengths and turn angles for the model
text:
Determining the initial step lengths and turn angles for the model
We have prepped our data. However, it is still not just plug and play. We need to investigate our data to fit general curves to our data to inform the model. We don’t need to do this, but it creates a more informed model based on the original data. We are trying to fit these data into two behavioral states, so we will want to inform the model with 2 curves.

hist(hmm_data_30$step, breaks = 20, freq = F, main = "Step lengths")
curve(dgamma(x, shape = 1.5, rate=0.9), n=200, add=TRUE, col="royalblue", lwd=4) #shape is how right-skewed the gamma curve is
curve(dgamma(x, shape = 1.9, rate=0.7), n=200, add=TRUE, col="cadetblue", lwd=4) #rate is how tall the curve apex is
curve(dgamma(x, shape = 2.2, rate=0.4), n=200, add=TRUE, col="navyblue", lwd=4)








#assign initial step length distributions
sl_init_mean <- c(2.2/0.4, 1.5/0.9) #initial means should be the shape/rate for both
sl_init_sd <- c(sqrt(2.2)/0.7, sqrt(1.5)/0.9) #initial standard deviations should be square root of shape/rate

This is a little subjective, but there is a good starting out point. The first curve encompasses the lower step lengths well. The second curve does not really add any more information either than including the step lengths that are longer. However, the third curve does this but also includes the higher amount of longer steps. So let’s go with the first and third curves
Now we do the same thing for the turn angles. However, we want the model to try to find states with opposite turn angles (turn 180 degrees vs straight). Therefore, we will play with the numbers a little.

hist(hmm_data_30$angle, breaks = 30, freq = F, main = "Turn angles")
curve(circular::dvonmises(x, mu = pi, kappa = 0.01), n=200, add=TRUE, col="royalblue", lwd=4) #mu is the mean direction of the angle

## Warning in as.circular(x): an object is coerced to the class 'circular' using default value for the following components:

The first curve is almost a straight line. But we want the model to try to fit 180 degree turn and straight. The second curve is straight ahead and the first is the turn around. It needs to be as close to flat as possible to fit the data the best.

mod <- fitHMM(data = hmm_data_30,
               nbStates = 2,

Looking at the step length and angle distributions, you can see a few things. State 1 is categorized by longer step lengths (average of 4 meters) and straight turn angles (0.007 radians, basically zero). State 2, on the other hand, has a much shorter step length (average of 0.9 meters) but a similar turn angle (-0.02 radians). YAPS position calculations
This is the general workflow for syncing receivers and running tracks in YAPS. We won’t be running this code in this workshop and in fact, this code does not work because the syncing fails. In reality, you need to play around with your sync data (including splitting up the time periods if there are “blackouts”, possibly removing receivers, and other adjustments) for the sync model to be successful. We will pick up the workshop with the positions that were calculated by the developer of YAPS (WOW!), Henrik Baktoft.

#Install and load required libraries

library(tidyverse)
library(TMB)
devtools::install_github(“baktoft/yaps”)
library(yaps)
options(digits.secs = 3)
#test to make sure YAPS will work
testYaps()
#load data
vue <- data.table::fread(‘data/detections.csv’, fill=TRUE)
hydros <- data.table::fread(‘data/hydros.csv’, fill=TRUE)
detections <- prepDetections(raw_dat = vue, type=‘vemco_vue’)
detections <- detections %>% dplyr::filter(!is.na(frac))
#now we have our 2 datasets needed!
#sync hydrophones/ #set parameters
max_epo_diff <- 140 #Should be a little less than half of your shortest sync tag delay (ours are 6 - 10 minute)
min_hydros <- 4 #minimum amount of hydrophones needed for each sync tag ping to be heard on. Start high, then go low
time_keeper_idx <- 13 #Receiver with the “best clock”
fixed_hydros_idx <- c(3, 7:8, 11, 13:17, 20:21) #Receivers that have the best known positions. The more, the better
n_offset_day <- 2 #1 or 2
n_ss_day <- 2 #number of times you want the model to calculate speed of sound a day. 2 is good, best to use water temp if you have it
keep_rate <- 75 #number of sync tag detections for each hydro X offset_idx combinations to keep. Keeps the model doable
#compile list of dataframes
RYAPS <- list(hydros, detections)
names(RYAPS) <- c(‘hydros’, ‘detections’)
RYAPS$hydros$sync_tag <- as.double(RYAPS$hydros$sync_tag)
RYAPS$detections$tag <- as.integer(RYAPS$detections$tag)
RYAPS$detections$epo <- as.integer(RYAPS$detections$epo)
RYAPS$detections$serial <- as.integer(RYAPS$detections$serial)

#check if it is good

#we are good. Let’s try syncing

#check quality of synchronization

plotSyncModelCheck(sync_model, by=“sync_bin_hydro”)
plotSyncModelCheck(sync_model, by=“sync_tag”)
plotSyncModelCheck(sync_model, by=“hydro”)
#success! there is only a problem of 6 using SHYAPS1. I think it is fine. save it
save(sync_model, file = ‘sync_model_4’)

#Now that you have the sync model, run the tracks

Calculating tracks
The most important part to set up for the HMMs is differentiating the tracks. This is where the second big decision comes in. How long do you wait between position before it is a new track? Depends on your array design, tag specifications, and the biology of your organism. We are using a cut-off of 5 minutes because our tags have an average burst interval of 20-40 seconds, meaning the fish would have to miss 10 detections (and therefore left the array).

title: Environmental Variables
text:
This section goes over what environmental variables we are using for our iSSFs. In this example, we will be using a two class (dense and sparse/bare) map of submerged aquatic vegetation (SAV) mapped using aerial imagery flown over our study site. The map was made using photointerpreted points to train a Random Forest algorithm on the spectral information within the aerial imagery. We will be using this map to also calculate spatial pattern metrics using the dense class of SAV, which are measures of composition and configuration of the seascape. Included in this section will also be the setup of the data for iSSFs, including calculating the “false” steps that the iSSFs use to determine habitat selection.
We will end up with 6 environmental variables: class of SAV, PLAND (Percentage of Landscape that the dense SAV class makes up), Edge Density (the density of edges of the dense SAV class), Patch Density (the density of patches of the dense SAV class), Division (a measure of likelihood that an adjacent cell is the same class as the cell you are calculating this metric on), and Mean Shape (a measure of how complex the patches of dense SAV are). title: Environmental Variables
text:
This section goes over what environmental variables we are using for our iSSFs. In this example, we will be using a two class (dense and sparse/bare) map of submerged aquatic vegetation (SAV) mapped using aerial imagery flown over our study site. The map was made using photointerpreted points to train a Random Forest algorithm on the spectral information within the aerial imagery. We will be using this map to also calculate spatial pattern metrics using the dense class of SAV, which are measures of composition and configuration of the seascape. Included in this section will also be the setup of the data for iSSFs, including calculating the “false” steps that the iSSFs use to determine habitat selection.
We will end up with 6 environmental variables: class of SAV, PLAND (Percentage of Landscape that the dense SAV class makes up), Edge Density (the density of edges of the dense SAV class), Patch Density (the density of patches of the dense SAV class), Division (a measure of likelihood that an adjacent cell is the same class as the cell you are calculating this metric on), and Mean Shape (a measure of how complex the patches of dense SAV are). title: Environmental Variables
text:
Extracting environmental data
We have our data in the format we need to both extract classes and run spatial pattern metrics on them. However, do you remember when we told you that the environmental data needs to match the resolution of your environmental data? Well, here is where it comes into play. For the extraction of SAV classes, we are going to use a kernel to calculate the class most present within a 10m x 10m square around each cell in our map. This mimics the 10m error we filtered by for our positions. We will then extract the class at each position using this new map.

#create a kernel for the map to calculate the majority class with
kernel <- matrix(1, nrow = 31, ncol = 31)

#Apply the kernel across all of the cells in the original map and plot it
rmap_kernel <- focal(rmap, w = kernel, fun = "modal", na.rm = TRUE)

plot(rmap_kernel) #it reduces the complexity, but is better for fitting the data. We will use the complexity of the original map to calculate spatial pattern metrics








#create a spatialpointsdataframe and extract from map
sr2 <- st_as_sf(sr, coords = c("x2_", "y2_"), crs = st_crs(rmap_kernel)) %>% terra::extract(x = rmap_kernel, y = ., ID = F) %>% bind_cols(sr) %>% 
  mutate(class = if_else(focal_modal == 1,2,1)) %>% drop_na() %>% dplyr::select(-focal_modal)

If the class is 2, it is dense SAV and if it is 1, it is sparse SAV/bare sediment. Now that we have our classes extracted, we are going to calculate some spatial pattern metrics. To do this, we are going to calculate the 5 variables brought up in the intro: PLAND, ED, PD, Divisionm and Shape_mn.
